questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a focused physical examination?
choices: To perform every possible maneuver at every visit
To answer questions raised by the history, general survey, vital signs, and differential diagnosis
To replace the patient history
To create a longer template note
questions.explanation: A focused examination is purposeful. It tests diagnostic hypotheses and helps determine safe next steps for a particular presentation.

questions.question: Which sequence is generally appropriate for an abdominal examination?
choices: Palpation, percussion, inspection, auscultation
Inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation
Auscultation, palpation, inspection, percussion
Percussion, palpation, auscultation, inspection
questions.explanation: Inspect and auscultate before palpation because palpation can change bowel sounds and increase discomfort. Then percuss and palpate gradually.

questions.question: Why is side-to-side comparison valuable during a focused examination?
choices: It makes every finding diagnostic
Asymmetry can be more meaningful than a vague global impression and helps establish the patient’s baseline
It eliminates the need for diagnostic testing
It is useful only for skin findings
questions.explanation: Comparing matching areas can highlight meaningful differences in breath sounds, pulses, edema, strength, sensation, temperature, and tenderness.

questions.question: A patient has reproducible chest-wall tenderness but also exertional chest pressure and diaphoresis. What is the safest interpretation?
choices: Reproducible tenderness completely excludes ACS
A musculoskeletal contributor is possible, but high-risk ischemic features still require appropriate urgent assessment
No further assessment is needed
The patient should receive only an NSAID refill
questions.explanation: A physical finding can support one diagnosis without excluding a dangerous alternative. Exertional symptoms and associated risk features must be integrated.

questions.question: Which finding most strongly requires emergency evaluation rather than routine completion of a neurologic exam?
choices: Chronic stable headache without new features
New aphasia, facial droop, or focal weakness
Mild muscle soreness after exercise
A stable old tremor already evaluated
questions.explanation: New focal neurologic deficits can indicate stroke or another emergency. Immediate escalation takes priority over extended outpatient examination.

questions.question: What is the best way to document a physical-examination finding?
choices: Use a copied normal template whenever possible
Describe location, symmetry, quality, timing, and functional effect using meaningful positives and negatives
Write only “abnormal”
Assign a diagnosis without describing the finding
questions.explanation: Precise descriptive documentation is reproducible and supports continuity. It is safer than vague labels or copied-forward findings.

questions.question: Which statement about a normal physical examination is most accurate?
choices: It independently rules out all dangerous disease
It must be interpreted with pretest probability, time course, patient risk, and examination quality
It means no follow-up is ever needed
It is more reliable than the history
questions.explanation: Physical findings have variable sensitivity and reliability. A normal examination may not exclude evolving or high-risk disease when the clinical picture remains concerning.

questions.question: A patient has a painful, pale, cool, numb, pulseless limb. What is the priority?
choices: Schedule routine vascular testing next month
Recognize possible acute limb ischemia and arrange emergency evaluation
Treat only with compression stockings
Document chronic edema
questions.explanation: Pain, pallor, coolness, sensory change, and absent pulses can signal acute arterial compromise, a limb-threatening emergency.

questions.question: Which action best supports a trauma-informed physical examination?
choices: Begin without explaining maneuvers to save time
Explain the examination, ask permission, provide privacy/draping, and adapt to patient needs
Avoid an interpreter when time is limited
Examine sensitive areas without offering a chaperone
questions.explanation: Consent, communication, privacy, appropriate draping, and adaptation improve patient safety, trust, and the quality of information obtained.

questions.question: A patient has unilateral calf swelling after prolonged travel and new dyspnea. Intact distal pulses are present. What is the best FNP reasoning step?
choices: Exclude DVT and PE because pulses are intact
Recognize that pulses do not address venous thrombosis risk; assess stability and follow an appropriate urgent VTE pathway
Diagnose cellulitis from inspection alone
Wait for bilateral swelling before reassessing
questions.explanation: Intact pulses do not exclude venous thrombosis or PE. The history, symptoms, stability, and appropriate diagnostic pathway guide care.
